newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon seen paying too much for TI unit.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon seen paying too much for TI unit.

text.p: Raytheon Co is paying too much for Texas Instruments Inc's missile and defense electronics assets, analysts said, but strategically the deal is a good fit.
"TI was a must win" for Raytheon, said one analyst who declined to be named. "That takes care of the first priority, to get that under their belt."
Nevertheless, he believes the price-tag, $2.95 billion cash for a business that is expected to have 1996 revenues of $1.8 billion, is too high.
"(Paying) one times sales was thought to be a lot. Anytime it's over one times sales, it's excessive," the analyst said.
A second analyst told Reuters, "On the surface, it appears that they are paying a pretty hefty premium."
He added, "I think it probably strategically is a good fit, but if you grossly overpaid..."
Raytheon and TI's Defense Systems & Electronics Group both manufacture missiles, sensors and seekers and aircraft and ground radar, and yet they do not overlap, analysts said.
TI is a leader in long-range precision strike programs, airborne radar and forward-looking infrared sensors.
Raytheon is a leader in air-to-air and ship-defense missiles, ground-based and shipboard radar, and has a major but weakening presence in missile defense systems such as the Patriot program.
Raytheon likely paid the high price to give it a step up in the expected bidding for General Motors Corp's Hughes Electronics Corp, analysts said.
The first analyst said Raytheon likely paid the hefty amount in order to conduct a cash transaction rather than a stock deal.
A stock swap with TI would complicate a Raytheon stock bid for Hughes, he said.
Northrop Grumman Corp is expected to be Raytheon's only competitor in the bidding for Hughes, analysts said.
The first analyst said a merger between Raytheon and Hughes would be a "great fit," combining the two companies' leadership in short-range missiles and radar.
"They're just so complementary in all their programs. They just duplicate each other," he said. "It would be nicely monopolistic in short-range missiles."
He predicted that, eventually, Hughes, Raytheon and Northrop would all merge into a single company.
Raytheon said the TI deal would be non-dilutive to earnings and would raise its total debt to more than $6.6 billion.
Analysts said they were pleased the deal would be non-dilutive and were not worried about the high debt level.
"Raytheon's always been very good at generating cash to retire debt," the first analyst said.
Raytheon spokesman Robert McWade told Reuters the company had a plan in place to pay down the debt in five years. He declined to say if Raytheon was a suitor for Hughes.
